maintopic: CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE
subtopic: ATTENDANCE OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the unanimous consent of the House I rise to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Next week a conference takes place in Victoria on the most important questions of patriating the Constitution and devising an amending formula. Additionally, other substantial constitutional questions will be discussed. The meeting will be in closed session. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has refused the request of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that the opposition parties be permitted to send observers. The Joint Committee on the Constitution has held more than 100 meetings in 40 cities and towns throughout the 10 provinces and in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and 1,000 Canadians have voiced their opinions in 5,641 pages of evidence. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale):
That this House is of the opinion that the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on the Constitution should be permitted to attend the Federal-Provincial Conference on the Constitution being held next week at Victoria as an observing body and that the committee should be permitted to give the conference the benefit of the knowledge accumulated by the committee at tremendous expense to the taxpayers of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in trying to assess the reasons for the government's injecting the profit motive into the Canada Development Corporation

June 9, 1971

as its primary operational motivation I noted three explanations. The first was to get rid of Crown corporations which have been an embarrassment to the government by virtue of their success. The second was the necessity of satisfying the investment interests of corporations in Canada which have funds they want to place somewhere. This would take care of both the first and second objectives. They could take the common property of all Canadian Crown corporations, such as Polymer, and turn it over to private investors. The third reason was to do something, after waiting around for eight years, so that the government would not be subjected to the embarrassment of having to put this matter in the next Throne Speech.
There seems to be a fourth reason. The fourth reason for having the profit motive in the Canada Development Corporation is really a form of political cowardice. It gets the government off the hook. If the Canada Development Corporation makes a decision that is not in the national interest and which is not approved by Parliament, the government can say that the objective of the CDC is to provide profit and therefore we cannot fault the government. The government is looking for an invisible hand to guide the Canada Development Corporation rather than to guide the objectives of national priority as determined by the Parliament of Canada. Judging from experience, this kind of political cowardice is not going to work. The government may get away with it for a little while, but it is not going to work.
We have had a similar experience in this respect. The government tried to operate the regional development program on this basis. Initially the program had hard and fast rules as to which areas would be entitled to assistance. The reason for adopting rigid formulas was to take the government off the hook with regard to making decisions as to the kind of development that should take place in various parts of Canada. That program had to be changed because it was too inflexible and did not work in the way that was promised. The government has now moved into a new area in respect of regional development. It exercises a much higher degree of discretion in terms of to whom grants shall be made and where development shall take place. When that change in the legislation was introduced in the House we pointed out that the government was embarking upon a dangerous policy. However, it was at least a policy that offered some form of success. The program has been notably successful. This area of discretion has given it any measure of success to which it can lay claim.
The same will happen to the Canada Development Corporation. It cannot be operated on a profit motive. You cannot avoid political responsibility when establishing a national development corporation. The government will learn this as the situation progresses. In discussing the Canada Development Corporation, one of the arguments of government members has been that to have the CDC under the jurisdiction of the government and subject to scrutiny by Parliament would be politically dangerous. They argue that people will exert political pressure on the government for development in certain areas
Canada Development Corporation
and to support some industries which are not viable, suggesting that social problems be looked after rather than economic problems.
What is Parliament for but to tackle problems of this kind? Surely if a proposal is put to the government that it does not feel is justified or viable, it can deal with the situation. The government does not have to buckle under every kind of political pressure. No government and no Parliament has buckled under all kinds of political pressure to which this Parliament must be responsive. We cannot turn over the responsibility of Parliament to something that is profit motivated, namely, the Canada Development Corporation. That is what Parliament is all about: it must be responsive to the political pressures of our society and not evade them as is being attempted through the Canada Development Corporation. This is what it really is, political cowardice and an evasion of governmental responsibility. It is an attempt to have a profit-motivated body do the thinking which the government is refusing to do on behalf of the Canadian people.
This debate is drawing to a close; we are summing up our positions. Those of us who have fought hard and long for a Canada Development Corporation are disappointed with the dishonest approach the government has taken in the creation of the CDC. We are certain the Canadian people will understand this and that eventually the kind of CDC our party advocates will stand in place of the emasculated thing that the government is presenting to this House.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. OBJECTS, POWERS. CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-219, an act to establish the Canada Development Corporation. Back in the beautiful and fabled province of Nova Scotia there is a story told around an area called Mahone Bay. In the days of the privateers a ship named the Teaser was being pursued. It sought refuge in Mahone Bay, where it was blown up by one of its crew who did not wish to be captured. Legend has it that today if you are in that area on a stormy and foggy night you can still see the ghost of the Teaser sailing before the wind with bare spars burning brightly in the fog. This is a ghost. Bill C-219 reminds me of the ghost of the Teaser because it has been around for a long time. Now it would appear that its skeleton has taken on some form and it has come back to the Commons.
Away back in 1963 the Speech from the Throne stated that the government planned to introduce a measure to establish a Canadian development corporation. Nothing happened during that session, however. In succeeding sessions the measure was mentioned but it was never introduced in the House. Finally, in 1971, a bill providing for the establishment of a large private corporation under government control has been introduced in the

June 9, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
Commons. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) describes the corporation in these words:
It will help develop and maintain strong Canadian-controlled and Canadian-managed corporations in the private sector and provide greater opportunities for Canadians to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada.
According to the Minister of Finance, the corporation is supposed to help shape and secure future Canadian development. It is to be a large-scale source of capital to create major new enterprises. It will join others in acquiring and rationalizing existing companies where competitiveness may be improved by merger, amalgamation or other corporate arrangements. These changes, the minister says, will reduce the risks of an undesirable degree of foreign control of the enterprises concerned.
The Minister of Finance states that the activities of the corporation will involve close relationship with the business and financial community. Able and experienced entrepreneurs will direct the corporation's operations to areas of critical importance in economic development-to high-technology industry, to resource utilization, to northern-oriented companies and to industries where Canada has a special competitive advantage. Generally, the CDC will not seek to exercise direct operating control of the corporations in which it invests and these corporations will not normally become CDC subsidiaries. Shares are to be sold to the public in competition with those of all other investment vehicles, and the bill specifically directs the CDC to invest for profit in the best interests of the shareholders.
The Canada Development Corporation is to have an authorized share capital of 200 million common shares without nominal or par value, and preferred shares amounting to $1,000 million with a nominal or par value not exceeding $1,000 each, divided into any multiple of $5. According to the minister, in order to enable the corporation to begin its operations without delay once the bill has been approved, the government will make $250 million available to it by undertaking to purchase its shares either directly or as an underwriter. Under this arrangement the government will subscribe $100 million in the first year and $75 million in each of the following two years. In addition, the bill provides authority for the government to lend up to $100 million to the corporation.
Again according to the minister, the Governor in Council will be given authority to sell to the CDC at a fair and reasonable price its interests in certain Crown-owned corporations such as Polymer Corporation, Eldorado Nuclear Limited, Panarctic Oils and Northern Transportation. The board of the CDC is to consist of between 18 and 21 directors, and until government holdings have been reduced to less than 50 per cent of the total issued and outstanding working shares the deputy ministers of the Department of Finance and of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will also be members of the board.
CDC shares will count as authorized investments for insurance and loan and trust companies, subject to existing federal law. The CDC will not be an agency or a
Crown corporation responsible to Parliament, but because it is created by an act of Parliament any change in its capital structure or in the powers of the corporation will require approval by way of a resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament.
In retrospect, we see that it took the government eight years in which to prepare this bill and present it to the House. I cannot help wondering why it has chosen this point in time to present the measure, bearing in mind that there are so many more pressing matters confronting us. Obviously, the government chose to wait eight years because it did not consider the establishment of the Canada Development Corporation essential to the economic development of the country. At the present time, when unemployment is high and inflation is still with us, it seems to me the bill provides a good diversion from the real problems of the day.
I cannot but wonder how many jobs will be created by the CDC. Where will it invest? How will it help curb inflation? The government gives the impression of being concerned about the economic development of the country, but it is by no means certain that the proposed corporation will be an instrument of such development. At the outset of its operations it will acquire four corporations, two of which are profit making, namely, Polymer and Northern Transportation, one which is losing a lot of money-Eldorado-and another, Panarctic, which is not yet making a profit. So much for development!
The assumption appears to be that an investment company established under government control will promote the creation of more capital for investment in Canada. I challenge this assumption on the basis that the government does not create capital. From my study of economics I conclude that additional capital can be created only by marshalling savings which would not otherwise be organized.
It is said the corporation will provide increased opportunities for Canadians to participate in the economic development of their country. I would remind hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that there are in Canada today many institutions which provide excellent opportunities for the small investor to participate in the economic growth of Canada. I am referring to the mutual funds. These funds are the custodians of sums exceeding the $2 billion proposed for the CDC and they are without exception eager to sell more shares to the public and enlarge their own investment operation.
The best expert advice and experience are available to serve the small investor in those funds. Shares are available at low cost, and in my opinion it is impossible to conceive an easier way in which Canadians may acquire a share in what the Minister of Finance calls the ownership and direction of business operations in this country. These funds hold enormous, sound investments in Canadian enterprises. Under legislation passed in 1960-I believe I am right in this-operating companies must derive 85 per cent of their gross revenue from Canadian investment sources if they wish to enjoy certain tax benefits.

June 9, 1971

It seems to me there can be no justification for the government entering into competition with existing business, especially when that business is competently and responsibly serving the public. The use of the enormous power of government in competition with Canadian business cannot fail to undermine confidence and create further uncertainty as to the future. The proposed arrangements for selling the stock of the corporation should be clearly understood.
When the shares go on the market the initial price will be $5 and no doubt all the resources of the government, all the advertising media to which it has access, will be marshalled to spur sales. Sales promotion will be extremely costly. Since the government's prestige will be at stake in the response of the public to the offering of the stock, we can expect the government to use every advantage open to it to push sales. The minister has plainly stated that support will also be sought from a wide variety of Canadian institutions including insurance companies, banks and trust companies. I consider this proposal dangerous in the extreme. I feel the government has no right to press such institutions to subscribe for stock in this new corporation. The government should not have the right to exert pressure on institutions to invest assets which are generally held in trust. There have been times in the past when governments have applied direct pressure on financial institutions to purchase their bond issues when facing difficulties in finding a market. In my opinion this type of tactic should not be permitted to be revived in any form.
The corporation is to provide financing for large Canadian enterprises which might otherwise be led to seek funds outside Canada with a consequent loss of ownership and control to non-Canadians. Just think what this particular clause means, Mr. Speaker. Any enterprise that can scare up a foreign takeover bid can then apply to the Canada Development Corporation and demand a bigger and better price. It seems to me that the corporation will provide a relatively captive market for businesses which their owners are anxious to unload at inflated prices.
It is also to be the function of the corporation to share in financing the initial development or expansion of large-scale industrial projects in Canada. It is said that existing channels in Canada are not adequate to finance large-scale projects, that a new channel must be created for this purpose. In my opinion this is simply not true. The fact that the yield on good equities at the present is around 3 per cent, compared with 5-3/4 per cent on government bonds and 8 per cent on five-year term certificates, clearly shows that Canadians are equity conscious and that existing channels are adequate to meet such needs if the investment is sound. Every experienced financier and businessman knows that the selection of risks is the essence of the success of any enterprise operating in the investment field. Good investments, including equities, are finding markets in Canada today. The riskiest of all would remain to be offered to the Canada Development Corporation.
Canada Development Corporation
If these are taken up and the corporation incurs heavy loss in consequence, I ask, Sir, will the Canadian taxpayer be required to bail-out the corporation? One of my concerns is the great pressures that would be exerted upon such a corporation in its selection of risks, that is to say, in the purchase of the capital stock of corporations engaged either in risk development of resources or marginal industrial projects. I can picture Members of Parliament, especially those on the government side, making special entreaties to the corporation on behalf of shaky enterprises in their constituencies. The responsibilities of management under those circumstances will be enormous. I cannot help but wonder where sound, experienced and competent management for such a mammoth corporation is to be recruited. It will certainly take a very long time to set it up with efficient management.
Another matter that puzzles and concerns me is the statement of the minister when he speaks of ensuring the independence of the corporation. The minister says that by selling shares to the public and having the shareholders elect some of the directors, the corporation will stand on its own feet, free of government control. At least the minister appears to recognize the inherent dangers that are implicit in the relationship between the government and the corporation, but the suggestion that the corporation will be independent of government is in my view a fantastic illusion.
It seems to me that if the treasury of Canada is to be called upon to purchase large blocks of the stock of the corporation, if it is required to purchase debentures of the corporation or to make loans to it up to an amount of $100 million, how then can the government and Parliament divorce themselves from their responsibility to the Canadian public for its operations? If Polymer and other Crown corporations are to be sold to the new corporation, how can the government and Parliament ignore their responsibility with respect to the operation of these Crown corporations? These are questions that have not been answered to date. Certainly they have not been answered in any of the debates that have taken place in this House.
In my opinion, neither the government nor Parliament can properly abdicate their responsibilities for such an institution, and the alleged independence of the corporation is a myth. If the day ever comes when this corporation shows a profit, can we be assured that the exigencies of the government, political or otherwise, will not enter into the declaration or withholding of dividends? In light of all these factors I cannot assume that this new corporation will operate independently of government. If the Canada Development Corporation grows to anything like the size pictured by the minister and invests substantially in the stock of other corporations, in my view its tentacles will spread like those of an octopus throughout the entire Canadian economy. When this happens we will be marching on the slippery slope to socialism from which there will be no return.
Another matter that puzzles me is this. Why have we not heard from the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Helly-er) or the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) in

June 9, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
the debate on this bill? These former Liberal cabinet ministers, when speaking outside this House are loud in their condemnation of the government and its policies, and rightly so. I know that confession is good for the soul, Mr. Speaker, but this chamber is the place to make your voice heard. This is the place to stand up and be counted. So I ask, where are these two former cabinet ministers this afternoon? Why are they not here to speak out against the policies of this government and to stand against the worst government our country has ever had?
There are other objections to this legislation that cause concern to serious-minded Canadians. For example, what kind of persons are likely to constitute the board of directors? It is evident that the government will appoint the initial directors. The minister has indicated that as the sale of the capital stock of the corporation proceeds, the government will retain the right to appoint a small proportion of the directors. Who can guarantee that these men will be appointed without regard to partisan considerations? Who can guarantee that they will not feel obliged to act as representatives and mouthpieces of the government in all the important decisions that are taken by the board? In fact, decisions on the scale to be taken by this board might conceivably at times involve the prestige, even the political life of the present government.
In theory, the shareholders will be free to elect the other directors. But if the policy pursued by the board should be embarrassing to the government as principal shareholder, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how long can the independence of the board be expected to continue? The stock of this corporation is to be redeemable at any time at the option of the investor. The price paid for common shares will be the closing sale price of the share on the principal stock exchange on the business day immediately preceding the date of giving notice of redemption, or if no bids or asking prices on the exchange are quoted for that business day the last closing sale price recorded on the exchange will be the price paid.
I would point out that to meet redemptions mutual funds are always in a position to liquidate high-class securities. Is this corporation to dispose of stocks in its portfolio on the market to meet redemptions? If so, in my opinion investments of the type that it is expected to hold would in many cases be unsaleable except at substantial loss. I believe that the size of this corporation and its position as a creature of the government will create a significant danger to its market operations. It could by its transactions influence and disturb the market in the most serious manner.
If the corporation purchases large blocks of stock of companies engaged in the development of resources or industries, is it going to be content to accept a minority position in such companies, or will it insist on holding control to protect its investment? In either case it would have to insist on the appointment of some directors, and in light of past performances these will all be Liberal supporters, which will give a political bias to this national corporation.
There are many other points of view which I could put on the record, but I believe I have said enough to indicate the reasons members of my party will not support this legislation when it comes to a vote in the House.

Mr. Speaker, having heard the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) and the hon. member who has just sat down, it seems to me that the days we have debated this bill will go down as black days in the House and the Canada Development Corporation will be the most awful thing to reach the Canadian people. If we listen to the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) we realize we have not yet reached the Valhalla their party would wish to accomplish through a Canada development corporation. Then we heard the minister state the government's position. I think it is about time I put forward the Liberal rationale behind this bill.
I direct the attention of the House back to 1962 or 1963 when discussion originated about a Canada development corporation. At that time Mr. Walter Gordon was the man who recognized some of our problems, and they were easily recognizable. One of the problems lies in why Canadian enterprise was not making headway compared with enterprise in the United States and other countries. It did not take long to find the answers. First, Canadian corporate law was not really suited to a wide distribution of shares. In most provinces the laws governing private corporations make it very costly for them to become public; and by and large we find that the market in Canada is speculative-people want to make a buck quickly and get out. It has not been an investment market. In the United States these corporations are under the control of the Federal Securities Exchange Commission and they operate under a definite set of laws. There are avenues through which a private entrepreneur can proceed. They can set up a syndicate and change a private corporation to a public corporation with wide distribution of shares, and at all times the minority shareholders are protected by the law. This was one of our ills.
Possibly the most difficult problem is that Canadians do not have investment capital. It was always presumed that money put away in savings as a result of hard work would be invested by Canadians in speculative or risk capital. It was found this was not so. The reason other countries have had greater success, especially the Un ted States, is that there is a fantastic accumulation of capital, going back to the whaling days, and the investment of that capital has generated more money for risk investment. It was also a different type of investment.
Canadian history of investment in enterprise with public distribution of shares has never been very good. By and large public investment has been in gold and uranium mines. These ventures usually wound up in the hands of a small group in Toronto or Montreal living on Bridle Path or Post Road making a few million dollars and everybody else losing a few hundred dollars. The

June 9, 1971

history of investment has not been bright. That is the reason for the thought behind the Canada Development Corporation, namely, to assist enterprise to develop. Since 1962 we have seen many examples of development corporations. They have existed from the Maritimes to British Columbia, and invariably few have been successful. I am speaking of the Newfoundland Corporation and the Maritime Corporation, among others. Very few have worked out and have been, if not unsuccessful at least not warranting further development.
Now the government has taken a new approach. It wants to develop an "instant" giant corporation. This, again, is not the answer because it loses sight of the original concept. I only intend to speak briefly but I would remind hon. members of some very cruel facts of the business world. A corporation or enterprise is successful because of the greed or selfishness of an individual or a small group of individuals. They want to make money and gain power. They want to gain an equity position in a structure which will be theirs. I put it to the House that corporations which have grown large and have lost control by a small group have usually wound up in bankruptcy.
There is no such thing as a corporation controlled by directors who have nothing to gam. Normally, enterprises work out well if the directors, the president, the vicepresident in charge of sales, advertising, and so on, have something coming to them; usually it is share equity. A president is appointed and told that if the enterprise is successful he will be given or will have the option to buy a hundred thousand or a million shares, whatever it may be. The desire for power and gain keeps these corporations growing and becoming successful.
Naturally, a government type of development cannot offer this incentive and unfortunately we wind up with apprehensions of the type expressed here today. We build a mediocre-type corporation which does not do the right thing. Creating an "instant" giant of the four or five Crown corporations which Canada now has will not solve the problem. All it might do is diffuse the ability we now have in this field.
This will be the last chance 1 will have to advise the parliamentary secretary and the minister that there is still a great opportunity for the Canada Development Corporation if we return to the original purpose, and that is to assist the development of enterprise. When you examine all these problems you find that there are no buyers for shares because the law does not protect minority shareholders. The history of Canadian investment is such that if you guarantee an investor a return on his money, he will buy. Canadians are not too easy with the money they have saved and they will not invest if there is risk.
The position of the Canada Development Corporation could be very strong if it adopted an approach similar to that of Central Mortgage and Housing in the mortgage field. The corporation should work toward a program by which it could examine new or existing enterprises. It could then set a certain premium to be paid by the
Canada Development Corporation
corporation. The corporation could put its stamp of guarantee on the shares. Then you would find growth.
This is not so strange. What I am really asking is that the small shareholder be put in the same position as large corporations. Many times I have invested money for clients on a short-term basis. I have purchased shares in large corporations. My clients were not willing to take the risk of a loss in the future. I went to a commercial banker and showed him a portfolio of shares which I required to cash six months hence. I asked how much it would cost to ensure the return of that amount of cash. He told me the premium, which I paid, and I was sure that six months later there would be at least that much money available. If there was more because the shares increased in value, my clients prospered: if there was less, the commercial banker took the loss.
What Canadians need, and must have before they invest in small enterprises and in the growth of an enterprise with a wide distribution of shares, is this type of guarantee. In a similar way the Canada Development Corporation could be very successful. It could examine and scrutinize all corporations and then approve some as good ventures. It could give the stamp of approval to sound enterprises which warranted a wider distribution of equity shares. The CDC should state to shareholders that it will give a guarantee on the premium.
If the contemplated approach is used, I do not think the future will be entirely black-but let us face it, it will not help the individual enterprise in Canada grow and there will still be the tendency for Canadian entrepreneurs to sell out to Americans who can do this sort of thing on a large scale. I urge the government to review its position within the structure of the act so that, as I have stated, it will have the power to use the CDC as an instrument to guarantee the shares of companies with a promising and worth-while future.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT ORDERS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. OBJECTS, POWERS. CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the bill I intend to be very short, which perhaps will be a surprise to some of my colleagues in this chamber. However, it is possible to be short and still be succinct and relevant.
As I rise to speak on Bill C-219 to set up the Canada Development Corporation there are many mixed thoughts in my mind. But in a philosophical sense, when we speak of the CDC in this day of the abbreviated form, whether it is IBM, GMC, 3-M or ATT-and now CDC-one can almost write a poem about abbreviated forms of iambic-pentameter time according to Shakespeare and everything else.
My concept of the CDC, which differs from that of several of my friends to the left, would be more in the form of another abbreviated phrase. I suggest that rather than "CDC" it could be "4S's". The four S's are "sop, sham and shabby substitute". Without going into detail, I believe the bill we are debating is a real sop to the nationalistic mood in Canada as in our 104th year we Canadians still try to define our national id, our national
24107-63J

June 9, 1971
Canada Development Corporation identity. I have nothing against that, but I question whether the CDC will produce some of the strength for the national identity that we all want.
It may sound fine to some intellectuals who think we are trying to buy back the past or preserve the future, but from the debate we have had we know there is disagreement in this House concerning whether the bill will do all that its backers and opponents would like it to do. It may be fine for the founding fathers of an independent Canada movement to point to the CDC and say it will help us control our economy and the integrity of the corporate enterprise and/or individual enterprise. But having read the bill and having listened to some of the debate in the House I say that because it does not go far enough-like my friends in the NDP-it is a sop to the nationalistic mood of this country.
The second "s" in my equation is that Bill C-219 is a sham to realistic economic planning because it attempts to balance the unbalanceable. It attempts to equate the motive for profit and all the enterprises where profit is the incentive. I am not against profit and certainly not against incentive, but I suggest that in this type of corporation which is supposed to do so much for Canada you cannot have the profit equation on the cash register on one hand and the necessity for development on the other. I suggest they are almost irreconcilable. I do not mean by that that you cannot have, through development, some profit. Obviously you can in the way private enterprise works in Canada, with all the state control we have.
My friends to the left may want more state control. I understand their point of view. I sympathize with it but I do not agree with it on all occasions. Through development may come profit, but you cannot have it the other way around if you are planning for the logical economic development of Canada. If your profit motive is the incentive for what you do, obviously you will remain outside a lot of the barren areas of Canada which need development.
My first "s" was a sop for the nationalistic movement in Canada and all the founding fathers, including Walter Gordon and other notables. The second "s" is that I believe sincerely-I do not like that word very much-it is a sham to realistic economic planning because you cannot balance profit with development. Through development may come profit, but through profit you may never have development. I have listened to the learned arguments of my friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and all those who have contributed so constructively to this debate, and I say that the last "s" in my 4S's is negative suggestion. That is admitted, but perhaps we in the opposition are cursed because we can only be negative from time to time. My last two "S's" are for the words "shabby substitute". I suggest the proponents of this bill are trying to perpetrate upon the Canadian public a shabby substitute for a relevant and viable vehicle for economic growth.
There is no doubt, as we look around and see all the indices, tables and so forth which are available from the Bureau of Statistics and other places, that we need economic growth in this country. But I question very definitely whether Bill C-219-giving it all the benefit of the doubt, having read all its terms and having heard the explanations of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and his parliamentary secretary-will produce the relevant and viable vehicle for economic growth which we so desperately need and anxiously await in Canada. Here I may differ very much from my friends to the left and perhaps many of my friends across the way who sometimes seem closer to my friends to the left than I am. That may be the case and they will have to live with it. However, my philosophy in the whole question of economic growth is that government should stimulate policies for development, and not develop legislative structures or legislative vehicles like the CDC in an effort to pretend that we have development.
We need over-all economic policies to move us up to the next step on the ladder. No one pretends we have reached our goal, but I suggest that in that step by step process up the economic ladder it is a shabby substitute to perpetuate Bill C-219 for the concept that was developed by the Walter Gordon's of Canada, and to pretend in this chamber that this bill even comes close to what the Walter Gordon's and the Alvin Hamilton's used to say about the necessity for legislation which would allow Canadians to develop our country and invest in Canadian industry.
It is anticipated that we will have a budget on June 18. I do not know why there is not yet an economic, across-the-board policy which would discriminate in favour of Canadians developing Canadian industry. During the life of the twenty-eighth Parliament it has been an accepted fact in committee hearings, because of the white paper, the evidence of the Minister of Finance and of many other Canadian economists, that there should be a capital gains tax in Canada. I am not arguing for or against that question today but I hope to have the opportunity when we debate the budget, depending on what the Minister of Finance does, to express my opinion that in this area alone there is potential for a viable policy for economic growth with a capital gains tax which would discriminate in favour of Canadians.
If I or other Members of Parliament-whether or not we have a pay increase-had any money left to invest after meeting our tax load, which is the same as that of the people in the press gallery and of people outside, although some misguided people might think we are protected, and wished to invest in a Canadian industry and realize a profit, it might be good policy for us to reinvest in a Canadian enterprise and not have to pay a capital gains tax on it. On the other hand, if I invested in an invidious U.S., British or French company I would have to pay a Canadian capital gains tax. In that way I suggest seriously we would be doing more for our economic development potential than is pretended in Bill C-219, which is supposed to develop a corporation to stimulate growth of Canadian industry.
Having said all that, I shall have no hesitation in voting against Bill C-219 because it is a sop to the nationalistic fervour of this country as we are trying to reach
[Mr. Nowlan.l
June 9, 1971

out and discover who we are, and I am all for that. However, I say it is a shadow and a pretence to think we will find solace in the CDC. 1 say it is a sham and it is not realistic economic planning because, as my friends to the left have said so well, especially the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) in his contribution to this debate, you cannot have the profit motive and the development necessity. If you turn them around, you may get some profit, but you will never get development if you use profit as the catalyst. Third, it is a shabby substitute for a relevant economic policy.
For those reasons, which I say add up to "4S's", sop, sham and shabby substitute, I will vote against this bill- and those are better reasons than many others which have been advanced for voting against other government bills. I wonder, in a philosophical way, if the CDC as it will be established under Bill C-219 is not another example of this government's preoccupation with culture and constitutions. I say this advisedly, not wanting to detract from the necessity of defining what Canadian culture is, whatever it may be, and it is an opening process, an evolving process. The culture that we have today is obviously far different from what we had 50 years ago and from the concept of the Fathers of Confederation.
In like fashion, when I refer to constitution I do not refer solely to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) and his government's preoccupation with an amendment to the BNA Act, with an amending formula or with the division of powers as between one provincial government and other provincial governments and the federal government. All these are very necessary and important- but in so many bills that we have had before us as legislators the government opts for the structure, for the Constitution, rather than for the reality which the Constitution is supposed to maintain.
You only have to consider the farm bill, Bill C-176, which was supposed to set up a framework to bring about a new millenium in agriculture in Canada. The minister responsible for the Wheat Board has contributed in part to that debate and so have hon. members on this side from time to time. But a bill like C-176, which creates a national farm marketing agency, by itself does nothing for agriculture. It is the producers who count in agriculture, and only then is there need for some regulation and control.
In like fashion we have here the CDC. Everyone talks about economic development and about Canadians owning Canada. I suggest that we go about it back to front, which is a kind way to put it, because the CDC by itself, and especially with the restrictions in this bill, will not do much to help the average Canadian to produce and participate in our economic growth. I almost hope I am proven wrong, although I do not think this will be the case. I submit that, for example, a change in the fiscal or the taxation policy could do more with a sweep of the pen than we are doing with all the words in this bill.
The government thinks that the government reorganization bill will make for more efficient government. I
Canada Development Corporation
question that. But before trespassing too far let me say that I hope I will have an opportunity to make a speech in this chamber on what I mean when I say this government is preoccupied with culture and with constitutions in various forms. Even though I am a member of a party that is opposed to the government, I went through the election in 1968, as the Prime Minister did, with the secret hope that we might accomplish in this chamber and in the country something that he was given a mandate to do. But I suggest that because of his preoccupation with constitutions, with culture and with all the structures that are involved, he has fallen by the wayside. Now he has to rely on sorties to Russia, China and other romantic spots in order to gild the lily. But that is another debate.
So far as Bill C-219 is concerned, I firmly believe the government should stimulate policies for economic growth and not create companies for the Canada Development Corporation to invest in, which is all we are doing here.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT ORDERS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT. OBJECTS, POWERS. CAPITALIZATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a long time members of the New Democratic Party and of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation before that, were in favour of establishing a national organization through which average Canadians could invest some of their savings to develop various segments of the Canadian economy. Socialists across Canada have for years supported that proposition. Now it is a matter of regret to us that the government, which has stolen so many planks from our program, has taken this particular plank and dressed it in such garb that it is unacceptable to those who believe in the principle that it is supposed to espouse.
It seems to me that only those Liberals who believe in political expediency, who believe in a return to themselves, could support the Canada Development Corporation as proposed in this bill. It seems to me that the CDC is unlikely to do much for the Canadian public despite the fact that the government has decided that its investment decisions must be profit-oriented.
I have been listening to the speeches made in this debate. I was particularly interested in the speech made last night by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hast-ings (Mr. Hees). When he was a minister of the Crown he was able to develop the philosophy that everybody in his department should get out and participate in the achievement of its aims and objectives. That was the Department of Trade and Commerce. He gave everyone in it a set of cuff-links inscribed to the effect that they should get off their fannies and go to work. If leadership is given it is well known that it will attract large-scale support. I think this was proven in that case.
I am not interested in a profit-motivated corporation. While I am not experienced in finance, not even to the extent of handling my own finances with any great ability, I was impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) who pointed out a number of

June 9, 1971
Canada Development Corporation important facts. The first fact he mentioned is that the Canadian public only invests in sure returns. Canadians do not want to speculate and, God bless them, I can realize why. For many years I was a miner. I saw Bay Street and James Street sell every kind of moose pasture in northern Ontario, moose pasture that did not have a trace of minerals in it. These people made their sales on the basis of all kinds of promises. I say that the gangsters in Toronto have financed Toronto by selling moose pasture in various parts of the country. Anyone who knew where those moose pastures were simply was not interested in investing money in that kind of game.
Other investors are those who want to invest a buck in a lottery, hoping, on a million to one chance or a hundred million to one chance, to win half a million dollars. The odds are fabulous but they are willing to speculate a small amount of money. But as the hon. member for York East pointed out, most people who invest have saved their money diligently, usually at some cost to themselves, and they put it into long-term, low-interest investments in the United States from which they are sure of getting their money back and are satisfied with a reasonable though low interest return.
I believe there is a new kind of investor emerging in Canada. These are the young people who have not had things so hard in earning their money. Of course, many young people now are having difficulty finding jobs through which to earn money. But young people are interested in the development of Canada, in the development of Canadian industry, in the development of businesses that will employ other young people. They would be willing to invest through a Canada development corporation such as that envisaged by my party.
Comments have been made about the investment of public money in the Maritimes, about particular investments in Newfoundland and in Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Nana:mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who is responsible for the development of many fine programs in Canada, told me that the government of Saskatchewan launched many developments through a provincial corporation similar to the CDC, and that less than 1 per cent of its investment was bad. The Saskatchewan investments were not made for the purpose of profit. They were made for the purpose of development. A large number of them had to do with utilities, the development of water, sewage and electricity services on which the return averaged 6 per cent, and on investments other than in utilities the return to the people of Saskatchewan averaged 16 per cent.
It is true that the provincial corporation lost money investing in a shoe factory. Why did it invest in a shoe factory? The reason was that the people of Saskatchewan were paying prices that were a third higher than those charged Canadians elsewhere for shoes. The people concerned admit that the Saskatchewan shoe factory produced a coarse product which did not meet the high standards set by Hart, Dack and other major shoe producers. But within a very short time the price of all shoes sold in Saskatchewan was greatly reduced, so the
local factory was allowed to fail. However, through the result achieved it did serve the people of Saskatchewan very well.
It seems to me that any Crown corporation interested in development should have as its first and prime interest not profit but the interest of the people it serves. Are we to get rid of Polymer simply because that corporation, in making money, is performing in a manner that goes against the government's philosophy? The government is not unhappy when the CBC loses money; it thinks that is justified. It is not unhappy when Canadian National Railways do not make money. We forget that we carry the original debt with the original interest and that we did not contribute to the original purchase of CNR. The government carries this debt and is pleased to see that railway lose money. Why, Mr. Speaker? It is a Crown corporation, and Crown corporations are supposed to lose money!
On the other hand, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse)-who I am sure is more of a Conservative than many of his colleagues-expressed the Conservative position with respect to this bill. He suggested that the government has no business monkeying with the financial development of this country. That, I thought, was a good Conservative position. The hon. member, however, does not remember that one of Ontario's largest Crown corporations was developed by Sir Adam Beck, an outstanding Conservative. He instigated development of a hydroelectric complex and wanted to manufacture cheap light bulbs which would burn forever, if that could be done. They were not to be like General Electric bulbs which will last 200 hours if you are lucky, or which will last 800 hours if you buy the better ones, if you are lucky. The company makes a commercial bulb which will save a man climbing a lamp post every few days because it may last up to 20 years. The hon. member does not realize that many Conservatives believed that people were more important than enterprises, than profits, and so on. They believed that people were the important factor and that governments should be more concerned about people and less about profits, prices or the other considerations that are involved in industrial profits.
The government has hamstrung this corporation. It will not be allowed to invest in corporations with a capitalization of less than $1 million. CDC is to take over and, I presume, operate corporations that are now successful. CDC will not be allowed to enter highly speculative areas and will not be allowed to go into areas of little or no profit. Mr. Speaker, the young people of Canada today believe that we should buy back Canada,, that we should get control of Canada, and they do not particularly sympathize with the big companies. I heard a representative from the pulp and paper industry on television last night saying that his industry has done much to control pollution, that this has cost a great deal of money and "nobody gives us any credit".
The Manitoba government is suing a pulp and paper company for about $35 million because the company

June 9, 1971

polluted a river 600 miles away. Sure the industry has done something about pollution. Our young people say to them, "You must either clean up the pollution or close down." They are also saying, "Let's buy back Canada." Many of us believe that this will be difficult. I am sure that even the most conservative person believes that it is possible for private investment to help the development of natural resources in a way that may mean that the returns, if there are returns, are not necessarily in the form of profits.
A long time ago we decided that many public utilities should not be in the profit-making field. Many of us believe that investment in development areas need not be considered as coming within the profit-making field.
I have heard all kinds of nasty remarks about the intrusions of government into the development of industries in the Atlantic provinces. I am an outsider so far as the Maritimes are concerned, although I have visited the maritime provinces a number of times in the past few years. I was in Nova Scotia a week ago and was surprised on visiting the town of New Glasgow, to see the terrific amount of development which has taken place in the area. Of course, the development was not like that of the suburbs of Toronto. The town was not like Calgary. It was not going ahead like Hamilton. But the change that has taken place since I was there previously is remarkable, Mr. Speaker.
It may be that the Atlantic Advisory Council and agencies of government which have participated in the development of industry in the area have not made money from some of these developments. In that way the agencies have not been successful. Nevertheless, in the sense that the community will grow and that industry will develop in future years, those agencies have been successful because the development could not have been possible without their intrusion.
Today a number of questions concerning Panarctic Oils were asked. Panarctic is a corporation 45 per cent owned by the government, the rest being owned by private industry. Why the government did not have the guts to make its share of that venture 50 per cent or 60 per cent, I do not know. They certainly did not take any chances on that investment. There is now a fabulous development on islands off the Northwest Territories, and they have only scratched the surface. This company has been successful, destructively successful. If the company develops the large area it has blocked off, it will be even more fabulously successful and the government will be embarrassed. So what has the government decided to do? The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) indicated today that Panarctic has begun farming out its business to Imperial Oil. Has Imperial Oil ever farmed out anything to Panarctic? Would it ever do that? I will bet they would not. Yet Panarctic is to farm out its business because it has become too successful and the government is embarrassed.
I hope that the investment which the public will make in the Canada Development Corporation will meet with success. The corporation ought to be successful. On the other hand, there ought to be some failures inasmuch as
Canada Development Corporation
the corporation should undertake development that private enterprise will not touch. The days when you could make a fast buck are gone. You cannot move into a forest, take out 10 per cent of the resources, destroy the rest, pollute the area, take your money and get out. You cannot go into a mine, take out some ore, if you are lucky, then take your money, invest it in another area and get out. Those days are finished. They are not finished by reason of the introduction of this bill. They are finished because our young people will not stand for the environment being ruined. They will not stand for the exploitation in which industry indulges.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there is a role for a Canadian development corporation. It should develop complexes in various parts of Canada and primarily in the primary resource areas. It should develop our resources, process them in a logical fashion and sell the finished product. Japan, the United States and most of the industrialized countries of Europe will be crying out for any raw materials that we can produce. I am aware that we have a surplus in uranium, copper and perhaps nickel. We certainly have a surplus of every agricultural commodity that we produce. However, this surplus situation is only temporary. Anyone who wishes to project the world demand for industrial development will realize that these resources must come from the countries which have the resources. Canada is one of these. In my opinion, as far as industrial processing is concerned, Japan will buy our iron, steel and other resources that can be developed to a degree. I do not suggest that we go into prefabrication in these areas, but that we finish the materials.
During my recent visit to Nova Scotia I was surprised when asked whether I was interested in subsidizing the transportation of steel to the province for the manufacture of boxcars. I said absolutely not. There is a steel mill in Nova Scotia. It can produce the steel that is required for these boxcars; they have foundry facilities and they can produce steel. If we provide the wherewithal by subsidizing the cost of moving sheet metal from Hamilton to Nova Scotia to prefabricate boxcars, why not prefabricate the boxcars being made in Hamilton?
Canadians are in a position to invest their savings in a corporation that will develop many of the resource-based industries which are desperately needed to provide jobs in areas in which it is almost impossible to create employment. Some of these projects will not be successful. They should not be successful; some should fail. There is no reason why the shoe factory in Saskatchewan should not fail. It does not matter a damn if it fails. It did not matter when the brick factory failed, because it served a purpose for the people of Saskatchewan; it enabled them to get the benefit of a better product at a lower price because the government was willing to develop it even at financial loss. Who carries the financial loss? It is all the people, and they have expressed a desire to do so.
Most of the resource-based development in this country could be developed in a highly successful way. It could

June 9, 1971
Canada Development Corporation
be a success for all the people of Canada. It would prohibit buying-out new resource areas and would prohibit their pollution. As sure as I am standing here, no Crown corporation of any description would be allowed to pollute to the degree of the exploiters of the resource-based areas of Canada.
I will oppose the Canada Development Corporation as a matter of expediency. I will oppose the proposition that it must be based on profit. I do so because the Canadian public demand the development of a corporation in which they can invest their money. Despite what is being said about the importation of foreign capital, Canadians invest more in the United States than Americans invest in Canada. Canadians will invest in finance companies, insurance companies, AT&T and other American corporations. On the other hand, American corporations invest very little in Canada. Most of the money they invest in Canada is returned to them in a very short period. The former Minister of Communications, the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), has said that our tax laws permit a write-off of between $1 billion and $2 billion per year through tax concessions. This means that investors who put their money into corporations in Canada will get their money back right away.
In my area Texas Gulf is being allowed a five-year tax-free period. This corporation will make millions of dollars in the first few years. It will probably be able to pay off its total capital investment with the money which is given to it in tax concessions. We have made concessions to industry and this has not worked. A large portion of Canada is not developed to any extent except in the basic resource development area. In the basic resource development area large sums of capital are being invested. A very small labour content is involved in that investment. In most cases it amounts to between $50,000 and $150,000 per job. I suggest that other industries dependent upon that resource will provide a very large labour content with much smaller investment.
As the Canada Development Corporation develops it must be made a Crown corporation. The government must control the development. This must be a partnership with the Canadian public so they will know where they can invest their money. As the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) pointed out, Canadians should be able to invest their money and get back as much as they invested. Canadians want to invest their money in the development of this country and be able to withdraw it when the need arises. They are not interested in making a huge profit on their investment. I am not talking about the speculators or the buyers of penny football pool tickets; I am talking about people who are interested in participating in the orderly development of Canada. They will participate if they are given an opportunity to have a say in how this country develops. This will not be done at a board meeting; it can only be done through Parliament.
The corporation must reflect the wishes of those who will be investing. These will be the people who wish to invest $1,000 or $2,000 in a corporation which will develop their country. They will do this on the basis of patriotism and the desire to have Canadian financing and, above all, Canadian control over our industries. For this reason they will participate in the development of the corporation. Canadians are not interested in investing in a corporation in which most of the companies have a hand, in which most of the companies will make their maximum investment, in which there will be a large amount of money and where the government will be making concessions so that the corporation will be successful. The only people who will benefit from that kind of corporation are those who have shares and participate as they would in any other company. That is not what Canadians want. They want an opportunity to participate in the development of Canada by Canadians, for Canadians. This is what they want and what they will demand.
If the government, with its majority, passes this bill it will find it will be unacceptable to the public. The public will demand that it be changed to make it their corporation so they can invest and participate in its development. The general public will demand that a corporation of this kind should build a pipeline through the Mackenzie Valley for the transportation of gas. Others would be able to use it on payment of a fee, but the Canadian people would own it. Thus, Canadian institutions responsible to Parliament would decide where the development would begin and where it would end. It would be in a position to control the amount of gas which could be exported. Such a corporation would have an immediate interest in building an oil line from western to eastern Canada so that all Canadians could benefit from the abundance of Canada's western oil and would have no need to depend on the whims of Nixon as to how much Canadian oil should be admitted and what would be traded in return for other concessions.
The young people of Canada are not tied to money as our generation is. They are not tied to the idea of bigness being necessarily good. They do not believe that corporations are bound to be right because they are large. They will be informed in their universities that most of the big corporations are extremely inefficient, that most of the leaders of big corporations are incompetent. We can see this from the names of those appointed to the boards of many of these corporations. There is no need for them to be efficient. They need only be big enough to buy up the competition. Then they can be as inefficient as they wish and still take all that the market will bear.
The new generation of Canadians has a different outlook, different aspirations. If the government is not smart enough to change, it will find that passing this emasculated document which is masquerading as a bill to develop Canadian resources, masquerading in the form of a crusader to buy back Canada, will not serve their interests in the least. If they think this bill will satisfy a much more enlightened electorate than we have had before, they are due for a big surprise.
I oppose this hoax on the Canadian public. I look forward to a day when more Members of Parliament believe Canadians should participate to a far larger

June 9, 1971

extent in their own development by contributing through their taxes and investing their money in this country so they can be masters in their own house. I look forward to that day and I believe it is not far off.

speechtext:
It is not my
intention to take much time on third reading, Mr. Speaker. I fully endorse the speech which my hon. friend has just delivered. He has very ably outlined the position of the New Democratic Party so far as the Canada Development Corporation is concerned.
Needless to say, our group is disappointed that no amendments have been accepted by the government. In the last two or three days we have moved a number of amendments which we believed would improve the legislation, but of course they were steam-rollered down. Unless the economic tactics of the government are changed, the only place in which it will have a majority will be on the floor of this House. The people of Canada are demanding that economic changes be made, and they are not getting these changes: they are not getting them through legislation, they are not getting them through this emasculated CDC bill we are now debating.
The legislation before us is woefully weak and it is deliberately designed to further weaken the small publicly-owned and controlled sector of the Canadian economy. It is a sop to private enterprise and a clear indication that the government intends to do little to arrest the increasing control which foreign ownership is exercising over the Canadian economy. In fact, the legislation proposes to phase out some of our most successful Crown corporations. It is an indication that the fire sale of our best Canadian resources will continue to be the policy of this administration. I have no hesitation in saying this. All the indications of the last three years are that this is to be the program of the government.
The legislation we are considering limits investment by the CDC to the shares of corporations in the $1 million and over bracket. The corporation will not be allowed to invest in smaller companies, to channel money into new resource projects which are needed to bolster our economy. This point has been raised time and time again in the debate. The corporation will be allowed to purchase four of our highly successful Crown corporations, Polymer, Eldorado Nuclear, Panarctic Oils and Northern Transportation Company. These corporations are now 100 per cent Canadian owned and controlled. They are being run efficiently and over the years they have returned substantial dividends to the Canadian people. Yet the government insists that the CDC be given a chance to take these corporations.
The fields which should be tackled are those which are foreign-dominated and foreign-controlled. As my hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has just said, the young people, the new generation will not stand for this type of nonsense very much longer. Either these changes will be brought about by the House of Commons or they will vote in people who will be ready to make the decisions necessary to bring our economy back under the control of Canadians. Why must we sell these 100 per
Canada Development Corporation
cent Canadian-owned corporations to the CDC? There will certainly be some investment in the corporation on the part of foreign-owned Canadian subsidiaries. Let us start investing in those secondary industries based on present resource development projects or in those sectors of the economy which are owned and controlled by foreign interests.
In my opinion the government has its priorities in a real mess. Its whole approach to economic problems over the last three years has been a tragedy for the Canadian people. The results of its economic program have been massive unemployment, inflation, a shortage of adequate housing, an environmental crisis and a tax structure which is completely outmoded. There are increasing indications of dissatisfaction with government policies. This is evident from the resignation from the cabinet of the former Minister of Transport and the former Minister of Communications; they resigned because of their dissatisfaction with the government's program and policies. This mood is spreading rapidly and the government should pay heed to it. As an example I would quote from the Toronto Star of June 4, 1971. This article, written about an economist who is disillusioned by the program presented by the government, reads:
Another economist, Max Stewart of the University of Alberta in Edmonton, who supported Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau in the last federal election, said, "I think Kierans' analysis is very sound, sounder than the one the government has."
But "it will have zero impact on Ottawa. They've closed their minds and they're impregnable."
There are dozens of other quotations I could make. The signals are up. Has the government lost all sense of reality that it does not recognize trouble when it sees it?

Some of the comments on foreign investment made by the hon. member for Duvernay are interesting. He pointed out that he felt investment stimulants or incentives have contributed more than any other single policy to the concentration of U.S. ownership that now exists in Canada. He went on to say:
-it is not what the Americans have done to us but what we have done to ourselves.
In other words, he is saying that it is the problems that we in this House of Commons have created which have caused the economic trouble in which we now find ourselves. He went on to point out that investment incentives apply precisely to those industries where foreign ownership is most	concentrated-in the mining,
petroleum and manufacturing industries. This is very pertinent to the bill and I should like to quote from page 11 of his speech as follows:
Investment incentives (depreciation, depletion, three year exempt mining income) apply precisely in those industries where foreign ownership is most concentrated, i.e. mining, petroleum and manufacturing. Total sources of funds for American subsidiaries in Canada in 1968 amounted to $2,611 million-
That figure is taken from a U.S. survey of current business.
Funds from the United States amounted to $127 million or less than 5 per cent. Within Canada was provided $1,027 million in net income, $864 million in depreciation and $539 million from Canadian financial institutions. Legislation to inhibit further inflows would be useless. Our tax laws are such that increasing ownership, takeovers and control of Canadian firms can be entirely financed from within our own economy.
What the hon. member for Duvernay is saying in simple language is that Canadian resources and industries are being bought up by Canadian money. And he is right. He then suggested remedies that could be taken. He pointed out that in 1968 less than 5 per cent of the funds of Canadian subsidiaries in Canada came from the United States, that over 95 per cent came from within Canada. This was also clearly indicated by surveys made last year by David Belli, an economist with the United States department of commerce who did a survey of U.S. subsidiary operations in Canada. He indicated that about 94 per cent of U.S. subsidiary investments in Canada are effected with Canadian funds, and that is in the records. He also indicated that in 1968 only $127 million were provided directly by parent companies or other United States financial institutions, and the ratio in the financing of U.S. subsidiaries in Canada in that year was about 19 to one in terms of Canadian and U.S. funds. For 1969 the picture is worse than that.
He also spoke about taxation, and this question ties in very closely with the bill since industry must make an adequate return to the Canadian people. The hon. member for Duvernay had some very interesting comments to make on taxation and produced some more than interesting tax tables which bear repeating. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Yours are words of wisdom and I appreciate them very much. I felt I had been keeping to the topic because all this is relevant. I was referring to some remarks of the hon. member for Duvernay in connection with foreign ownership. I have one more quotation and then I shall deal with one or two tables. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) can relax a little, and he need not be as embarrassed as he should be about the remarks of the minister. I quote from another statement about the results of tax policies in Canada as follows:
If foreign ownership dominates the mining and petroleum industries, our tax system has clearly invited this concentration. We have not only extended a warm invitation to foreign capital, but we have told it where to go. If you invest in the service industries, we say, you will have to pay taxes on 87 per cent or 90 per cent of your profits. On the other hand, in metal mining you will only have to pay on 13 per cent and in petroleum on 5.7 per cent of your profits. The invitation says in effect, "come and gut us".
There are one or two tables I should like to deal with. They were raised in the House the other day. They are worthy of repeating because they should indicate to hon. members and the Canadian people the trouble we are in as far as resource development is concerned. Table No. 2 given by the hon. member for Duvernay in his speech refers to metal mining. The hon. member pointed out there was a book profit of $1,707 million from metal mining, yet the taxable income was only $222 million. Only 13 per cent of the total book profit was taxable. That was not the total tax taken in; it was the amount of which tax was payable. There were $1.5 billion of book profits in the metal mining industry on which Canadians received no return. It is in this area that we are referring to the CDC and investment in Canadian resources. Some thing like $1.5 billion could not be touched; it went out of the country. And you wonder why people are fed up, sick and tired of the programs and policies this government had laid down over the years. It is not improving on them.
Let me refer to mineral fuels, which include oil. This is a pretty touchy point. There were $795 million in book profits in the mineral oil industry and we only taxed on $45 million. Only 5.7 per cent of the total book profits in the mineral oils industry was used as the tax base. We never received $45 million out of $795 million; the $45 million was the total on which we based corporate taxes. The government calls this a fair share, when other groups of individuals and corporations in the country are receiving a shellacking from this government. No wonder there is an uproar from one end of the country to the other.
Then we come to the category of "other mining." There was a book profit of $374 million. The taxable income was $120 million or 32 per cent. Let me move to the end of the table, where we find the retail trades. This is very interesting. What is the composition of the retail trades? I suggest it is a host of little businesses from one end of Canada to the other. Out of $1,620 million, this industry was taxed on $1,445 million, or 90 per cent of its book profit. There is a big difference. We come to the other end of the scale and find that for mineral fuels,

We are fed up with policies that allow this to go on and we are asking for changes. That is why we raise these issues.
Here we are in this country, with from 600,000 to
700,000	people unemployed in addition to students who cannot find jobs. Thousands of students cannot find even a summer job. I suggest the reason behind this can be found in the resource development programs of this government. We have allowed corporations to come in and get a stranglehold on the key resources of our country. They go into the north, to the mining areas and extract the choice minerals. Almost without exception they are shipped out of Canada without any fabricating taking place. This is the sort of thing we suggest the Canada Development Corporation should change. We should be fabricating these materials. The fabrication of our raw materials should take place within the confines of Canada. This would give jobs to Canadians, in a Canadian setting. The measure before us will not accomplish that objective. The CDC will not go into these fields and return the ownership of the economy of Canada to Canadians.
We take objection to this measure and we are speaking out now. We urge the government to consider some of these clauses and even now accept some of the amendments we have suggested. There is a host of arguments, as my friend suggested, which can be saved for the budget debate. Again I suggest through you, Mr. Speaker, that members of the Liberal government should, for goodness sake, have another look at the legislation. Let us get something in here that will give Canadians the hope that we will start moving into these fields and gradually regain control of our economy for the people who live in this country.
At the rate we are going, so far as investment and resource development programs of this government are concerned we are becoming squatters in our own country. Again, in closing I urge that the government take another look at this measure before we vote on it and it is passed through the House in its present form.
