Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
The government says that interest rates have fluctuated. Following policy lines which had been pursued in the last several years, the government proceeded to amend other items of legislation including the cash advance legislation which to all intents and purposes was intended to provide interest-free cash advances, as its earlier title suggested. However, by way of amendment and the introduction of new clauses to the bill, the minister managed to slip in provisions whereby the government could collect interest from the day on which an advance was first requested. We argued against this proposition. We felt that interest-free cash advances should be continued because cash sales were limited and a requirement for cash existed. A similar requirement for cash was evident two years ago.
When speaking on June 7, the minister told us that $272 million had been taken out on 112,000 advances, if my memory serves me correctly. As I have said, through the amendments there has been introduced a change in the method of collection. Instead of injecting or infusing money into the western economy, the government suggested to farmers that they avail themselves of the cash advance legislation and take out loans. The farmers took out loans. I understand that some 50,000 loans were requested but that only $90 million or $92 million was taken out. While the government was professing that this was a method of infusing money into the western economy, it brought in restrictions or applied impositions with respect to the method by which advances would be collected.
Secondly, the interest aspect reared its ugly head. Although the minister told farmers that the quickest and easiest method for them to obtain money was by utilizing the cash advance legislation, the farmers ran into difficulties. In the last few years conditions have been difficult. A depression was brought on through a crop failure. Then because of wet weather farmers were faced with the added burden of drying their grain. In addition we have record low sales. Last year's sales were the lowest in 15 years. Sales were so poor that farmers, in a desperate attempt to obtain cash advances, may in some cases have overestimated the amount of grain they had available.
One must know the complexities of the grain business to realize that two grain bins of identical volume and size may contain different quantities of grain. The quantity will depend on grade, and so on. Thus, one bin may contain perhaps twice as much grain as another bin of the same size and volume. The grain in the two bins may be of different grades and the grain in one of the bins may be damp. On the basis of past history one would think the farmer could accurately estimate what he had. On delivering the grain, however, he might find that it is out of condition and that the dockage and shrinkage is much more than he expected. It is very possible that farmers legitimately overestimated. He can only work on estimates. There is no formal inspection; the farmer simply signs an affidavit. When this happens, the farmer can be in the position of having overestimated and taken an advance on grain far in excess of what he actually

Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act had. In most of these cases the farmers are back in business next year.
The government started dabbling in the cash advance repayment field for their own purposes, to pull them out of a political situation that was very embarrassing. There was a desperate need for cash. The government came out with a double amount of cash advancement. The sole purpose of doubling cash advances was for the government to get the money back into the economy as quickly as possible. In doing so they have changed the rules of the game. In changing the rules of the game the government may have intended to confuse the producers. Now that the producers have availed themselves of these new conditions, the government says, "We have caught you in the act. You had your hand in the cookie jar. You have to start paying interest in a different way than you have been accustomed to in the past."
The method applied was that when a producer committed himself to delivery of a six-bushel quota, if and when the quota was available, he had to deliver in a reasonable time. If he did not deliver when called upon by the Wheat Board, he was told that he was in default and that 6 per cent would be applied on the amount of the advance that was not repaid. The rules have now changed because the government wanted them changed. The government wanted that infusion of cash into the economy.
On June 7 the minister said that the producers had availed themselves of this cash advance program. The government now says that if the producer is in default, even by a very legitimate overestimation, he has to repay the cash advance in the same way as if he had borrowed the money from a bank. The principle is that the government wants to get its money back in a hurry. This is the prime purpose of the legislation. I could see that some parts of the legislation were working contrary to the original intent. I felt that some of it was tying the hands of the producers.
There are three types of grain on which cash advances are made, wheat, oats and barley. If, for example, I had
2,000	bushels of wheat that I could commit to the Wheat Board, I could take a cash advance on it. I may also have some oats and barley for sale. The amount on which I might be able to take an advance would be $6,000. If all I wanted to commit to the board or mortgage, was $2,000 on grain which I was prepared to deliver to the Wheat Board, the advance could be made. If all I am committing to the Wheat Board is my wheat, I should be able to take an advance on only that type of grain. I may have reason for wanting to keep my oats and barley available. The barley could be used as a cash crop.
Under the former practice, if one delivered a load of wheat, half the amount of the sale would normally be deducted in repayment of the cash advance. There may be a quota available and I may want to deliver a full load of barley because of my cash requirement. I may not want the Wheat Board to get its money back immediately. This should not be the prime requisite. The people of Canada should not have to work in the interest of the
government. The government should be working in the interest of the people. Our thinking has become twisted somehow.
One of my amendments in committee was to the effect that it should be possible for producers to have a cash crop which they want to deliver. I do not suggest that producers should take an advance on only one grain. My amendment suggested that they should have the option of taking an advance on three grains. The minister said this would disturb a principle. The principle was interest free cash advances. Now it is interest-full cash advances. The original principle was to benefit the producer. The principle now is that the producer should benefit the government because the government is in a hurry to get its money back.
The government says, "We gave you an advance and, boy, you had better give it back tomorrow." This is why the committee, including government members, supported the amendment I made in committee. The minister then said, "What is the matter with you? The people have to work for the government. You are supporters of the government, but you have lost sight of the principle." Over the years they may have had the right slant on what is required of the government and what should be given to the government, but the principle now is that the government comes first. Regardless of what the minister said, I felt it necessary to correct a shortcoming in the amendments presented by the government.
I met the minister half-way in one of my amendments. Under the amendments suggested by the government a producer may have paid back everything except ten bushels and still be found in default. On an advance of $6,000 which you may have taken you could technically be found in default and have to pay interest on the whole amount at the interest rate the Governor in Council might suggest. The minister shakes his head, but technically this could be done. Maybe he would say, "Well, we would bend over backwards in a case like that. It would probably not be worth making a big issue out of it." But technically that is the effect of the amendment the minister introduced.
If a farmer had taken an advance of $6,000, he would still have to pay, even though he had delivered $5,000 worth of grain and had repaid $5,000, interest on $6,000, according to the changes. I have suggested in my amendment No. 4 that when a delivery is made and you have repaid $5,000, from there on in if you are found in default you should be prepared to pay interest. I did not say one should not pay any interest. I was quite prepared to go to the extent of accepting the minister's own suggestion that it should be at a rate which the Governor in Council himself had prescribed. That is bad enough. But I was willing to concede a point and say that from the date the last delivery was made, whether it was made at the end of January-or if you took it in faster, so much the better-or any date, from the date when the final delivery was made on which an advance was repaid I could be called upon and told, "You should have delivered, but you did not. We can legitimately say you have no more

grain." If that situation should arise, then interest should be charged.
But what has happened in the past? Even if the final delivery of grain was made in January, and there was no more quota until the end of March and when the quota opened up and the producer did not deliver, the board informed him he had ten days or so in which to deliver. If he did not deliver in that time he was found in default and he paid interest from March. So as a compromise I said, "Let's go half-way." But the minister wants it all. The government is hungrier than some of the people who took the advance because they did not have the money. They do not take an advance unless they have to.
The repayment performance under the old scheme was that only about 1 per cent of the advances were not repaid. And that was only because of some extreme difficulty, changing hands or sometimes fire or loss of grain from flooding, and so on.
Then suddenly the government changes the rules and says, "We have to get away from this. We are a high-interest government, so let's apply the principle all over the place. After all, this works hand-in-hand with our original intention. We will make it a little tougher for the farmer to get an advance. It will not be interest-free. He will have to pay interest." That adds to your cost, and we all know the net result. It's the last straw that breaks the camel's back, and combined with some of the other philosophies projected by this government one finds it easy to understand why they would want these changes. It is easy to understand why they would want to reject an amendment which even some of their supporters felt was necessary.
Mr. Speaker, there was great emphasis placed on the committee system and I, along with many members of the committee from all sides of the House, applied myself to the point where we even sat all night on occasion. Genuine ideas came forward from all sides; government supporters do not have a prerogative in this respect. I have sat in committees where it required the minister to tell his supporters what they should approve and what they should not approve.
This practice makes a farce of the committee system. It frustrates the work of committee members and the work of Members of Parliament who feel they have a contribu-

tion to make either on the basis of experience or because of having listened to briefs submitted by people who genuinely think they are doing something to change legislation. Some farm organizations go to great lengths to get the information. They go out into the country and get as much information as possible from individual producers. Then they compile the information, co-ordinate it and work together.
The executive sit around and say; "What is our final position to be? What is our submission to be?" Committees hear representations and some of us, even on the opposition side, can understand what the briefs suggest. We suggest amendments and on the basis of those amendments we think we are helping to improve legislation. But it seems that the government, or a group of civil servants who are hard at work advising the minister-who may or may not understand the situation- what will be good for him, and telling him he had better not accept any more amendments from the opposition, ignores our suggestions.
